In this block, collective efficacy beliefs about solving the environmental crisis (from van Zomeren, Leach et al., 2010) were assessed. The scale consisted of four items in a non-randomized order ranging from1 = "Not at all" to7 = "Very much" (e.g., "When thinking about the environmental crisis, I think, as humans, together we are able to stop this ongoing crisis"). The internal consistency appeared to be very good (ω = .82).

Pro-Environmental Ingroup Identification

The complete 14-item version of ingroup identification was used to assess participants' identification with environmental concerns (e.g., "I feel a bond with people concerned about the environment"; from Leach et al., 2008). The rating started from1 = "Completely disagree" to7 = "Completely agree". The internal consistency was very good (ω = .91), and the items were in random order.

Pro-Environmental Ingroup Norms

We assessed descriptive and injunctive pro-environmental group norms (Ajzen, 2006).

The scale contained six items with responses ranging from one to nine. For instance, "Most people concerned about the environment, who are important to me, think that I should take care of the environment (by recycling my waste, promoting public transport, and purchasing local products, for instance)" ranged from1 = "I should not" to9 = "I should". The internal consistency for injunctive norms was good (ω = .79), and the internal consistency for descriptive norms was very good (ω = .87). Items were presented randomly.

Pro-Environmental Responses

In this block, four scales were presented and displayed in random order. We included three scales of collective action intentions. We assessed collective action intentions adapted from van Zomeren, Spears et al. (2010), such as "I would like to do something together with others to fight the climate crisis". It included three items arranged in a randomized order, and responses were on a 7-point scale ranging from1 = "Not at all" to7 = "Very much". Internal consistency was good (ω = .79). We measured collective action intentions with a 7-item scale from Landmann & Rohmann (2020), including items such as "Support campaigns for environmental protection". Responses ranged from1 = "Not at all" to7 = "Completely" and the order of the items was not randomized. Internal consistency was very good (ω = .87). We used a 2-item scale from Hoppe et al. (2023) to, again, assess collective action intentions (e.g., "I am willing to take part in collective actions to conserve nature on Earth, e.g., demonstrations"). This scale ranged from1 = "Not true at all" to5 = "Completely true". The internal consistency was very good (ω = .83), and the two items were randomized. We also assessed collective pro-environmental behaviors from Stanley et al. (2021). Participants were asked how frequently they engaged in eight collective pro-environmental behaviors over the past 12 months (e.g., "Signed a petition online or in person") from0 = Never to100 = at every opportunity. The internal consistency was very good (ω = .83), and the items were not in random order.

Eco-Emotions

All measures within this block were presented in random order. We included five eco-emotional scales. One adapted from Ojala (2015), assessed two factors: constructive climate hope (e.g., "Because politicians in more and more countries take climate change seriously"; ω = .78) and denial climate hope (e.g., "Because I doubt that there is any change in the climate"; ω = .73). This measure used a 7-point scale from0 = "Not at all" to6 = "Very well" and consisted of 11 items placed in a non-randomized order. Another scale assessed warm-glow (e.g., "I expect to feel good when I behave environmentally friendly"; from Jia & van der Linden, 2020) with four items on a 7-point scale from1 = "Completely disagree",7 = "Completely agree". Internal consistency was very good (ω = .83) and items were in a non-randomized order. Next, we measured awe (e.g., "In the wilderness, I feel awe and reverence"; from Bethelmy & Corraliza, 2019) using six items arranged in non-random order on a 5-point scale ranging from1 = "Completely disagree" to5 = "Completely agree". Contrary to the original scale, the exploratory factor analysis revealed a two-factor structure.

The first four items were related to awe regarding wilderness, and the last two were related to fear of wilderness. To measure awe, we selected the first four items and calculated the internal consistency, which was moderate (ω = .69). We also included a measure for the emotion of being moved, or kama-muta (e.g., "moved"; from Landmann & Rohmann, 2020). This was a 3-item scale with responses from1 = "Not at all" to7 = "Very much", and the order was not randomized. Internal consistency for this scale was very good (ω = .83). For the final scale, we used the Environmental Trait Affect-Questionnaire (ETA-Q; Hahnel & Brosch, 2018), consisting of 18 items on a 7-point scale from1 = "Completely disagree" to7 = "Completely agree" (e.g., "I feel GRATEFUL for our planet and its nature"). The order of items was not randomized. This measure assessed five factors. The first one is positive baseline affect, which is the disposition to experience positive emotions about the current state of the environment. The second one is positive outcome affect, which is the disposition to experience positive emotions as a result of actions that positively impact the environment.

The third one is negative outcome affect, which is the disposition to experience negative emotions as a result of actions that harm the environment. The fourth one is obstruction affect, which is the disposition to experience negative emotions when we intend to act environmentally friendly but are forced or feel forced to act in a harmful way. The last one is coercion affect, which is the disposition to experience negative emotions when they feel compelled to act pro-environmentally (or feel blocked from acting anti-environmentally).

Internal consistencies ranged from good to very good across factors (ω = [.74, .89]). From this scale, we also used the items gratitude and pride as single-item measures. Additionally, we included three single-item measures for inspiration, enthusiasm, and compassion on a 7-point scale from1 = "Completely disagree" to7 = "Completely agree" (adapted from Hahnel & Brosch, 2018). The items were not in randomized order.

New Environmental Paradigm

We used the New Ecological Paradigm questionnaire validated in French (NEP; Fleury-Bahi et al., 2015). This scale included 15 items ranging from1 = "Completely disagree" to5 = "Completely agree" (e.g., "Plants and animals have as much right as humans to exist"). Internal consistency was good (ω = .77), and the item presentation was not randomized.

Ecological Dominance Orientation

We assessed participants' Ecological Dominance Orientation (EDO; Uenal et al., 2022) on a slider from1 = "Less hierarchical" to7 = "More hierarchical", indicating participants' preference concerning the relationship between humans, animals, and the environment.

Demographics

In the last block, we measured participants' age, gender, religiosity, political affiliation, education level, residence place, and belief in environmental crisis. The last one consisted of one item: "I believe in the environmental crisis and that human activity is at least in part responsible for it". It served as a data analysis exclusion criterion to avoid measuring different constructs. Each measure in this block was not randomized and presented in the order described above. Finally, participants were thanked, and an email address was displayed if participants had encountered any issues or wanted to know the results.

Results

Primary Analysis

Correlational Analysis

We pre-registered several hypotheses regarding the correlations between eco-emotions and pro-environmental collective action intentions (H1). First, we expected a moderate to high correlation with warm glow and confirmed this hypothesis by finding a correlation of r = .33, p < .001. Next, we hypothesized low to moderate correlations with awe and compassion, which was supported by correlations of r = .23, p < .001, for awe and r = .35, p < .001, for compassion. Finally, we expected no to low correlations for hope, being moved, gratitude, inspiration, enthusiasm, and pride. Contrary to this hypothesis, we found moderate to high correlations for these eco-emotions: r = .26, p < .001, for hope; r = .45, p < .001, for being moved; r = .49, p < .001, for gratitude; r = .27, p < .001, for inspiration; r = .44, p < .001, for enthusiasm; and r = .40, p < .001, for pride. Not pre-registered, we also calculated correlations for positive baseline affect and positive outcome affect with collective action intentions. We respectively found a moderate (r = .26, p < .001) and a high (r = .52, p < .001) correlation. These coefficient interpretations are based on Cohen's guidelines (1988), which, on average, remain consistent overall today according to recent analyses (Lovakov & Agadullina, 2021).

Mediation Analysis with Ingroup Norms

Following the correlational analysis, we hypothesized a mediation (H2) where the relationship between eco-emotions and pro-environmental responses would be mediated through ingroup norms (Fritsche et al., 2018). We chose to present the three mediations with the highest indirect effectsfoot_0 . The three mediations presented below differed only in the independent variable X, which was either pride, warm glow, or enthusiasm. In each case, the mediator M was injunctive ingroup normsfoot_1 . We chose injunctive norms as they seem to be a better predictor than descriptive norms (Schultz et al., 2007; Smith et al., 2012). However, this difference is not clear-cut, as some evidence also suggests that descriptive norms are a more reliable predictor of pro-environmental behaviors than injunctive norms (Farrow et al., 2017).

Lastly, the response variable was pro-environmental collective action intentions. It is important to note that we deviated from the pre-registration by using an alternative dependent variablefoot_2 . We did so because mediated effects were stronger with this other dependent variable. This deviation will be considered in our conclusions and interpretations.

We first tested whether pride was positively associated with collective action intentions and found a significant effect (path c), b = 0.46, SE = 0.04, 95% CI [0.38, 0.54], t(481) = 11.19, p < .001. We then examined the mediation hypothesis by conducting a joint-significance test (Yzerbyt et al., 2018) include zero; we could therefore conclude that taking into account ingroup norms significantly reduces the variance between enthusiasm and pro-environmental collective action intentions, though the effect size was still small, b = 0.09, SE = 0.01, 95% CI [0.05, 0.13]. A summary of the mediation models reported here can be found in Table 5.

It is important to note that many of our mediation paths violated the linear regression assumptions of normality and homogeneity. This limitation will be addressed in the discussion section. parentheses.

Secondary Analysis

Multiple Regression Analysis

As this study is exploratory, we pre-registered seven other hypotheses to test assumptions that stem from the SIMPEA theory (Fritsche et al., 2018). According to this model, ingroup norms, ingroup identification, and collective efficacy beliefs have an impact on pro-environmental responses and interact with each other. That is to say, for example, the higher we believe ourselves to be collectively effective concerning the environmental crisis, the higher we will engage in pro-environmental responses, and this depends on the level of identification with the group. Of course, the opposite is possible as well as with ingroup norms. To test these hypotheses, we ran the following and pre-registered linear model in R:

To begin, this model explains 48% of the total variance (R² adj = .48). We thus found a significant positive main effect of collective efficacy on pro-environmental collective responses (H3) while controlling for age, political affiliation, and gender, b = 0.08, SE = 0.03, t(434) = 2.25, p = .02, partial r = .10, 95% CI [.01, .19]. The stronger the individuals' belief that collective action can bring about meaningful environmental change, the greater their intention to engage in pro-environmental collective actions. Furthermore, we found no positive main effect of injunctive ingroup norms on pro-environmental collective responses (H4) beyond the effect of our covariates, b = 0.04, SE = 0.03, t(434) = 1.19, p = .23, partial r = .05, 95% CI [-.04, .14]. Next, after controlling for age, political affiliation, and gender, we found a significant positive main effect of ingroup identification on pro-environmental collective responses (H5), b = 0.53, SE = 0.04, t(434) = 13.13, p < .001, partial r = .53, 95% CI [.46, .59]. That is, the more people identify with people concerned about the environment, the more they intend to engage in pro-environmental collective actions. Ultimately, we found no statistically significant interaction terms (H6, H7, H8, and H9). To be noted, we found that political affiliation was negatively associated with pro-environmental collective action intentions while controlling for all other predictors, b = -0.22, SE = 0.03, t(434) = -5.78, p < .001, partial r = -.27, 95% CI [-.35, -.18]. This means that the more people move to the right wing, the less people intend to do pro-environmental collective actions.

Mediation Analysis with Ingroup Identification

The strongest finding from this auxiliary analysis testing SIMPEA's (Fritsche et al., 2018) assumptions was the positive effect of ingroup identification. Given our model's complexity, with 10 predictors, we considered this effect robust (zero-order r = .64, 95% CI [.59, .69]) and pursued further exploration based on this finding. The following analyses were therefore not pre-registered. Theoretically, SIMPEA suggests that emotions should enhance ingroup identification, which in turn predicts pro-environmental responses. This is because, when the self is perceived as threatened, individuals rely on their ingroup to mitigate the threat, leading to endorsing group-based motivations and cognitions that promote responses (Fritsche et al., 2018). Based on this framework, we tested several mediation models with eco-emotion as the predictor (X), ingroup identification as the mediator (M), and collective action intentions as the response (Y). Like in the main analysis, we reported the three mediations with the strongest indirect effectsfoot_3 . Our results indicate that the relationships between eco-emotions and pro-environmental collective action intentions were moderately to strongly mediated by ingroup identification (see Table 6). These findings support SIMPEA's proposition that ingroup identification mediates the relationship between (eco-)emotions and pro-environmental responses. Regression coefficients are standardized, and their standard errors are in parentheses.

Discussion

The purpose of this study was to explore the relationships between positive and self-transcendent eco-emotions, group-based processes, and pro-environmental responses (intentions or self-reported behaviors). Four main findings emerged. To start, we conducted a correlational analysis based on several hypotheses regarding the strength of the correlations between various positive and self-transcendent eco-emotions and pro-environmental collective action intentions. Overall, we found moderate to high correlations, which align with the current literature and support that eco-emotions are medium to strong predictors of pro-environmental responses (Brosch, 2021), especially positive and self-transcendent eco-emotions in this case.

Next, concerning mediations with ingroup norms, the indirect effects were very small. This suggests that other variables may account for the relationship between eco-emotions and pro-environmental responses. In addition, for some regression paths, the residuals were not normally distributed or homogeneous, thus violating linear regression assumptions that can increase type I or type II errors (see Tomarken & Serlin, 1986, for non-homogeneous variances). It is also important to note that we deviated from pre-registration by using the dependent variable that gave the greatest indirect effects. Therefore, these findings must be interpreted with caution, and we conclude that SIMPEA's assumption that ingroup norms mediate the relationship between emotions and pro-environmental responses is only partially supported. Future research with a more controlled design and more precise variables relevant to a defined study context is recommended.

Subsequently, we used a linear regression model to test SIMPEA's assumptions regarding ingroup norms, collective efficacy beliefs, and ingroup identification. According to the theoretical model, each of these variables is expected to have a positive effect on pro-environmental responses individually, as well as interact to exert a positive effect on pro-environmental responses. We found no evidence for a main effect of ingroup norms, although we found a positive significant effect of collective efficacy beliefs on pro-environmental collective action intentions. Additionally, there were no significant interaction effects, including the three-way interaction. These findings are somewhat unexpected and do not align with SIMPEA. These effects may have gone undetected due to distributional asymmetries in certain independent variables. For instance, the distribution of injunctive ingroup norms exhibited a pronounced negative skew. The lack of observations in the lower range of the scale may have limited our ability to detect this interaction. Overall, by visualizing other variables' distributions, we found having a very educated and left-wing sample. Sampling issues may be at stake here, threatening sensitivity and power.

As the last finding, we did find a main effect of ingroup identification. Exploring this path, we still relied on what SIMPEA (Fritsche et al., 2018) suggests and tested an additional assumption -a posteriori and not pre-registered -of this theoretical model. That is, ingroup identification would mediate the relationship between emotions and pro-environmental responses. Indeed, facing an environmental threat would elicit ethnocentric responses (e.g., emotions and motivations) that would fuel ingroup identification, which in turn would affect pro-environmental responses (Fritsche et al., 2018). We found that ingroup identification moderately to strongly mediated the effect of positive eco-emotions on collective action intentions, supporting SIMPEA's assumption.

Further, several limitations that have not yet been mentioned so far have to be addressed. First, we could raise several criticisms of self-reported measures, such as the inability of participants to assess their own behavior, or between-and within-participant differences in response interpretation (but see Lange & Dewitte, 2019, for a discussion on pro-environmental behavior measures). However, these criticisms have recently been challenged by comparing self-reports with the alleged advantages of implicit measures (Corneille & Gawronski, 2024). A second limitation concerns causality. While mediation models usually contain unidirectional arrows, our study is correlational, so we cannot at any time infer any causal effect between our variables. Finally, another limitation involves the measures used, some of which were ad hoc and may lack a comprehensive psychometric assessment. This limitation affects the reliability and validity of our conclusions and presents an obstacle to cumulative science (Lange, 2023, p. 618; Lange & Dewitte, 2019, p. 97).

Overall, despite finding large and significant mediation effects of pro-environmental ingroup identification on the relationship between positive and self-transcendent eco-emotions and pro-environmental collective action intentions, this hypothesis was not anticipated beforehand. This present study was exploratory, and our degree of freedom was quite large. In order to significantly reduce this degree of freedom, we sought to replicate and extend this mediation hypothesis within a new, more controlled study with an experimental manipulation of a self-transcendent eco-emotion and with an actual pro-environmental behavior measure.

Study 2

This second study aims to manipulate a self-transcendent eco-emotion and, contrary to Compassion is conceptualized as witnessing the suffering of a person, which creates a need to help that person reduce their suffering (Goetz et al., 2010; Lazarus, 1991; Stellar et al., 2017). For the present study, we extend this definition to the suffering of the natural environment and label it as compassion for the environment (Bellemin et al., 2026). Some authors categorize compassion as positive (Keltner & Cowen, 2021) and others as negative (Zaremba et al., 2024). We relied on Shuman et al.'s (2013) work on valence and conceptualized compassion as implying two micro-valence distinctions. Despite being more of an unpleasant feeling (Bellemin et al., 2026), compassion is also related to moral goodness by the need to help the suffering object.

Manipulating compassion appears to have an impact on pro-environmental intentions (Pfattheicher et al., 2016, Study 2). In-depth analysis showed that manipulated compassion and support for government climate action are mediated by both beliefs in anthropogenic drought and political ideology (Lu & Schuldt, 2016). Compassion also mediates the relationship between loving-kindness meditation and sustainable decision-making (Engel et al., 2020, Study 2). However, the relationship between compassion and pro-environmental behaviors has never been studied in the light of group-based processes and with an empirically validated behavioral measure.

Therefore, according to SIMPEA (Fritsche et al., 2018), we expected that participants in the eco-compassion induction condition will produce higher donations compared to participants in the control condition (H1), and this would be mediated by pro-environmental ingroup identification (H2). That is to say, the effect of eco-compassion induction on donations would decrease when controlling for pro-environmental ingroup identification.

Also, as proposed in SIMPEA, ingroup identification interacts with ingroup norms. We thus expected a positive interaction effect between pro-environmental ingroup identification and pro-environmental ingroup norms on donations. Specifically, pro-environmental ingroup identification would be positively associated with donations (H3), and this effect will be stronger when pro-environmental ingroup norms are high (H4). As in the first study, we chose injunctive norms to test this hypothesis. Lastly, according to Landmann (2020), the repetition of eco-emotional episodes related to environmental crises, over time, creates affective attitudes toward these crises through the process of affect generalization (Paolini et al., 2006).

And these affective attitudes predict pro-environmental behaviors more consistently than eco-emotional induction. We operationalized this theoretical hypothesis by pre-registering a predicted interaction effect: specifically, we expected that the effect of compassion induction on donations will be higher for participants with a higher environmental trait affect score (the positive baseline factor; Hahnel & Brosch, 2018) compared to those with a lower score. In hindsight, however, the way we tested Landmann's (2020) hypothesis was not the right approach. Landmann's hypothesis (2020) actually invites a different question: do individual differences in eco-emotional traits (measured as stable dispositions) predict pro-environmental behaviors beyond any effect produced by an eco-emotional induction procedure? We therefore expected a positive effect of positive baseline affect on donations beyond the effect of eco-emotional induction (H5). This new way of testing the hypothesis was not pre-registered and arose during data analysis and interpretation.

Methods

We pre-registered this study in OSF: https://osf.io/3yf24/overview?view_only=68620794a1634f78ac80b6198369d60e

https://osf.io/3yf24/overview?view_only=68620794a1634f78ac80b6198369d60e. Any information that was not preregistered will be explicitly mentioned in the article. The data set, analysis scripts, and other related documents can be found on the following link: https://osf.io/ngmdp/overview?view_only=88978a08707c4925a8ebce1d451664f2.

Power Analysis

To determine our sample size, we selected the main hypothesis where we expected the smaller effect size -that is to say, the mediation effect (H2). To do this, we used a Monte-Carlo power analysis for indirect effects (Perugini et al., 2018; Schoemann et al., 2017). We defined arbitrary coefficients for each path of the mediation analysis. For an indirect effect of 0.05, 91% power, and an alpha level of .01, we need 375 participants (see the power analysis section on the OSF page). We anticipate potential exclusions and therefore added 25 participants to this sample size, leading to a targeted sample size of 400 participants.

Sample

In total, we recruited 400 French participants in February 2025. They were recruited via Prolific Academic (n = 360) or personal contacts (n = 40). Participants from Prolific were paid £2.5. Eleven participants met our exclusion criteria and were removed from the final sample. We did not pre-register an exclusion criterion for excessively long completion times, by mistake. Thus, we also removed two participants who took more than an hour and a half to complete the experiment, a duration considered excessive both by our team and according to Prolific's rules. We therefore ended up with a final sample of 387 participants (Mage = 31.8, SDage = 10.4, 48.3% identified themselves as women, 50.6% identified themselves as men, 1% identified themselves as others).

Procedure & Measures

The experiment was conducted entirely on Qualtrics in French. At the begining of the experiment, we told the participants that this research contains two separate studies to save time for data collection. The first study is on participants' relationship with the environment, and the second study is a number identification task. This information was provided to minimize potential demand effects (Corneille & Lush, 2023) by preventing participants from linking the emotional induction to the subsequent behavioral task (see below). After giving their consent, participants were randomly assigned to one of the two experimental conditions.

Either the control group (n = 200), where participants had to recall a recent memory, or the eco-emotional induction group (n = 187), where participants had to watch a video inducing eco-compassion. This eco-emotional manipulation previously showed induction validity (Bellemin et al., 2026). Following the experimental manipulation, we assessed participants' pro-environmental ingroup identification (ω = .90; adapted from Leach et al., 2008), participants' collective efficacy beliefs (ω = .91; adapted from van Zomeren, Leach et al., 2010), participants' descriptive and injunctive pro-environmental ingroup norms (ω = .85 and ω = .76 respectively; adapted from Ajzen, 2006), and participants' Ecological Trait Affect (ω = [.79, .88]; Hahnel & Brosch, 2018). These measures were presented in random order.

Next, participants were invited to do the number identification task, which was the Work for Environmental Protection Task (WEPT; Lange & Dewitte, 2022). This task was designed to measure an actual pro-environmental behavior. Specifically, in this task, participants had the choice to do a monotonous task (i.e., number identification) in favor of donations to a pro-environmental organization (OroVerde). In other words, the more participants completed pages (WEPT performance), the more they donated. Participants had the choice to complete up to nine pages (instead of 15 pages in the original task), with either 40, 80, or 120 numbers on the page. The amount of donations was either 0.10, 0.20, or 0.30 euros and was fully crossed with numbers on the page. At the end of this task, the participants saw on the screen the amount of money they had accumulated to donate to the organization.

Then, we asked participants demographic questions in a non-random order: gender, age, religiosity, political affiliation, education, residence place, household income, and belief in the environmental crisis. Finally, we told the participants the real purpose of this experiment and thanked them for their participation. Additionally, an email address was displayed if they had encountered any issues or wanted to know the results. On average, the experiment lasted 21.8 minutes (SDduration = 10). In addition, a total of €465.5 in donations (observations removed included) was given to a pro-environmental organizationfoot_4.

Results

Given five a priori hypotheses, we used a Bonferroni correction, leading to an alpha level of 1%.

Main Analysis

First, we hypothesized that the induction of eco-compassion would produce a higher WEPT performance compared to the control condition (H1), and this effect would be mediated by pro-environmental ingroup identification (H2). We first tested whether there was an effect of the experimental manipulation on the WEPT performance and found a non-significant effect (path c), b = 0.06, SE = 0.10, t(375) = 0.66, p = .509, d = 0.07, 99% CI [-0.20, 0.33]. Then we examined the mediation hypothesis by carrying out a joint-significance test (Yzerbyt et al., 2018). Path a testing the effect of eco-emotional induction on pro-environmental ingroup identification was non-significant, b = 0.26, SE = 0.10, t(375) = 2.57, p = .010, d = 0.27, 99% CI As anticipated, we observed violations of regression model assumptions and performed a mediation analysis for nonparametric inference (Imai et al., 2010). However, we also found no statistically significant effects for either hypothesis. We also applied a square root transformation on our dependent variable, but again, no statistically significant effect was found. Finally, we used negative binomial regression models and found no significant effect at the level of 1%.

Auxiliary Analysis

Next, we hypothesized that pro-environmental ingroup identification is positively associated with WEPT performance (H3) and that this effect depends on the level of pro-environmental ingroup norms (H4). To test these hypotheses, we ran the following linear model in R:

As hypothesized, we found that pro-environmental ingroup identification was positively associated with WEPT performance, but this effect was not statistically significant at our corrected alpha level, b = 0.11, SE = 0.05, 99% CI [-0.01, 0.24], t(371) = 2.12, p = 0.033. Nonetheless, this effect was significant at the level of .05, suggesting underpower. We therefore calculated the zero-order correlation between ingroup identification and WEPT performance and found a significant and positive correlation, r = .17 6 , p < .001. For the fourth hypothesis, we did not find a statistically significant positive interaction effect of pro-environmental ingroup norms on the relationship between pro-environmental ingroup identification and WEPT performance, b = -0.003, SE = 0.05, 99% CI [-0.13, 0.12], t(371) = -0.07, p = .940. For the final hypothesis (H5; incorrectly operationalized in the pre-registration), we expected a positive effect of positive baseline affect on WEPT performance beyond the eco-emotional induction effect. To test this hypothesis, we performed a multiple regression with WEPT performance as the dependent variable, positive baseline affect as the predictor, and eco-emotional induction as a covariate. We found no statistically significant effect of positive baseline affect on WEPT performance, while controlling for eco-emotional induction, b = 0.07, SE = 0.05, 99% CI [-0.17, 0.62], t(384) = 1.44, p = .14.

As for H1 & H2, we applied a square root transformation on our dependent variable, and no statistically significant effect was found for H3, H4, and H5. We also used negative binomial regression models and found no statistically significant effect as well.

Supplementary Analyses

As none of our a priori hypotheses were clearly confirmed, we explored the data in depth to better understand these results. Therefore, the following analyses were not pre-registered. As they are purely exploratory, we set our alpha level at the standard level of significance in psychology: a = .05.

To start, we analyzed the data, selecting only participants with a hit rate above 90% and a false alarm rate below 10% (and again with a hit rate of 80% and a false alarm rate of 20%), and found no statistically significant effects supporting our hypotheses, except for ingroup identification (H4) on WEPT performance, b = 0.18, SE = 0.06, 95% CI [0.05, 0.31], t(277) = 2.89, p = .004.

This means that potential participants who did not perform the WEPT well did not hide any effect except for ingroup identification, which was more significant after all. In addition, we ran the same analyses but without participants who completed the task entirely (i.e., who donated the maximum amount of money possible). We obtained the same results as just before, but this time, ingroup identification barely reached significance, b = 0.10, SE = 0.05, 95% CI [0.002, 0.20], t(217) = 2.01, p = .045. Therefore, participants who performed each trial of the task did not hide any effect except for ingroup identification again (H4).

We then referred to how the task was developed and validated. First of all, we investigated whether our task worked well. That is to say, it produced a real trade-off between personal investment and environmental benefits as intended by the original authors. Indeed, according to how the authors developed and validated the task (Lange & Dewitte, 2022 , 2023), we tested on our sample and implemented design (three number conditions instead of five) their two main hypotheses: The odds of completing a WEPT page decrease when the numbers on WEPT page increase (H1); the odds of completing a WEPT page increase when the donation amount increase (H2). We ran a first mixed-effects logistic regression with the R package lme4 (Bates et al., 2015) Finally, we visualized almost every variable of our study and calculated its correlation with WEPT performance. In Table 7, we reported Spearman's correlations since WEPT performance was not normally distributedfoot_5 . Demographically, we found that we had a young, very educated, left-wing sample. However, none of these variables were significantly associated with WEPT performance. We also found that ingroup identification, descriptive ingroup norms, and injunctive ingroup norms each significantly accounted for variance in WEPT performance. As for the environmental trait affect dimensions, positive outcome affect, negative outcome affect, obstruction affect, and coercion affect were significantly associated with WEPT performance separately; this contrasts with the non-significant effect in the fifth hypothesis.

Discussion

This second study aimed to examine whether the induction of eco-compassion predicted engagement in an actual pro-environmental behavior and whether this relation was mediated by pro-environmental ingroup identification. We found no evidence for the first hypothesis and even less for the second. We also hypothesized that ingroup identification would be positively associated with pro-environmental behavior, and injunctive ingroup norms would moderate this effect. The data at the corrected alpha level supported none of these hypotheses, but the main effect of pro-environmental ingroup identification was statistically significant at the conventional level of five percent, suggesting underpower.

Beyond the effect of eco-emotional induction, we expected a positive association between positive baseline affect and WEPT performance, but found no evidence for this hypothesis either.

As we used the same dependent variable for every hypothesis, explanations can directly come from the task itself. In supplementary analyses, we first visualized the distribution of completed WEPT pages per participant and observed a negatively skewed distribution. This skewness creates two related issues: violation of regression model assumptions and ceiling effects. We used non-parametric analyses, a square root transformation on our dependent variable, and negative binomial regression models. Still, no statistically significant effect was found for each of the five hypotheses. Therefore, the alternative hypothesis that violations of regression model assumptions could have hidden an effect can be excluded. Next, no significant effects were found after removing participants with an average hit rate below 90% and a false alarm rate above 10%, except for the association between pro-environmental ingroup identification and WEPT performance. The alternative hypothesis that our results can be due to some participants who did not perform the task well can be potentially excluded. Neither any significant effects were found after removing participants who performed the task entirely, except for the same association between pro-environmental ingroup identification and WEPT performance. Finally, we found that the odds of completing a WEPT page decreased with increasing page size, and the odds of completing a WEPT page increased with increasing donation amount. These results confirm that the task did work as intended originally by producing a real trade-off (Lange & Dewitte, 2022). The alternative hypothesis that the task did not work well can be excluded.

As the WEPT was validated, showing a real trade-off between personal investment and benefit for the environment, associations with related constructs, and scope sensitivity (Lange & Dewitte, 2022; 2023), construct validity seems not to be at stake. Perhaps the shortening of the original task could explain why we had such a ceiling effect. As participants are notified in advance about how many pages they could complete in total, this could have had an upstream influence on participants' motivation for the task, as the number was not the same in our study compared to the original task (nine pages vs. fifteen pages, respectively).

That is to say, notifying participants that they can complete up to nine pages could have led to a greater proportion of participants completing the task than notifying them that they can complete up to 15 pages. In addition, we also had a very educated and left-wing sample. This finding reveals sampling issues and could explain the ceiling effect in our behavioral task.

Last, as part of our supplementary exploratory analyses, we found positive associations between pro-environmental ingroup identification, pro-environmental ingroup norms, and WEPT performance. This means that the more people identify themselves as pro-environmental people, the more they donate to a pro-environmental organization. Equally, the more people report strong pro-environmental ingroup norms, the more they donate to a pro-environmental organization. This supports the model SIMPEA (Fritsche et al., 2018), but not substantially. Indeed, the association between collective efficacy beliefs and WEPT performance and the expected interaction between pro-environmental ingroup identification and pro-environmental injunctive ingroup norms were non-significant. Moreover, we found associations between positive outcome affect, negative outcome affect, obstruction affect, coercion affect, and WEPT performance. This means that the more people have a strong disposition to experience positive emotions as a result of actions that positively impact the environment, the more they donate to a pro-environmental organization. In the opposite way, the more people have a strong disposition to experience negative emotions as a result of actions that harm the environment, the more they make donations. Also, the more people have a strong disposition to experience negative emotions when they intend to act environmentally friendly but are forced or feel forced to act in a harmful way, the more they donate. And the more people have a strong disposition to experience negative emotions when they feel compelled to act pro-environmentally, the less they donate to a pro-environmental organization. Despite no significant correlation with positive baseline affect, these relationships are consistent with Landmann's (2020) hypothesis that affective attitudes towards the environmental crises explain pro-environmental behavior more than eco-emotional induction alone. Future studies should inspect how exactly these environmental traits are related to pro-environmental responses. Previous findings showed that environmental decisions depended on the interaction between environmental trait affect and gain or loss framings (Hahnel & Brosch, 2018; Tarditi et al., 2020).

Overall, the present study did not replicate the mediation effects found in Study 1.

Two differences distinguished this study from the first one. First, we experimentally manipulated a self-transcendent eco-emotion. Second, the response measure was an actual pro-environmental behavior and not only self-reported intentions. Testing whether inducing eco-emotions impacts pro-environmental responses may require first studying it with shorter tasks or with behavioral intentions. In order to replicate major mediation effects found in Study 1, we aimed to replicate these findings with the same study design and the same dependent variable. This is the objective of Study 3.

Study 3 (Replication of Study 1)

The present study aims to replicate the results of Study 1, closer to a conceptual than to a direct replication. Specifically, we aim to replicate the hypothesis that the positive relationship between positive and self-transcendent eco-emotions and pro-environmental collective action intentions is mediated by pro-environmental ingroup identification.

According to the Social Identity Model of Pro-Environmental Action (SIMPEA; Fritsche et al., 2018), environmental crises would threaten the self, and people would then experience a range of different emotions. To protect the self, people would rely on a group to mitigate the existential threat, and this would produce group-based motivations to act.

However, this hypothesis, rather exploratory in the model, is debatable since the emotions directly emerging from a threat are not supposed to be positive. Therefore, SIMPEA does not seem to account for positive eco-emotions. In our view, environmental crises induce emotional experiences triggered by the individual's concern for the environment. These emotional experiences activate the individuals' pro-environmental identity. This highlights their belonging to a group, a pro-environmental human collective. This group identity generates motivations to act. Thus, pro-environmental group identification would predict intentions to act and capture (mediate) the effect of affective experiences on collective action intentions (Thomas et al., 2012; Thomas et al., 2009). This new hypothesis guides the present replication study.

Methods

We pre-registered this study in OSF: https://osf.io/gxb4q/overview?view_only=b07db5409b5a4213bf596567f79f8d68

https://osf.io/gxb4q/overview?view_only=b07db5409b5a4213bf596567f79f8d68. Any information that was not preregistered will be explicitly mentioned in the article. The data set, analysis scripts, and other related documents can be found on the following link: https://osf.io/cu4ag/overview?view_only=6aca7b4f5040413e96db70c25c0cfe75.

Power Analysis

To determine our sample size for this replication, we took the smaller indirect effect found in our mediation models of Study 1. That is to say, the indirect effect from the model with awe as the independent variable. By using Schoemann et al.'s (2017) shiny app, we set the parameters according to our data in the original study with awe, but for paths a, b, and c', we used the lower bounds of the 95% IC. Assuming an alpha level of .001 (adjusted for multiple testing) and a targeted power of 90%, the required sample size would be 500 participants.

Sample

Data collection lasted from November 2025 to March 2026. Unlike what was pre-registered, we did not recruit only via Facebook, but also via LinkedIn, Instagram, and distant personal contacts. Given that data collection was very slow, we also recruited psychology students in exchange for course credit. Due to time constraints, we ended data collection at a total of 1,005 responses. Applying our pre-registered exclusion criteria, we ended up with a final sample of N = 461 (Mage = 36.5, SDage = 16.4, 73.1% identified themselves as women, 25.5% identified themselves as men, 1% identified themselves as others).

Procedure & Measures

The survey was carried out on LimeSurvey. The different blocks of measures were displayed in random order, except for the consent and demographics blocks. We made some changes from the original study by removing some measures and adding some new ones (see pre-registration for more details). Two new measures integrated in this survey were translated into French using a forward-back translation method (Sousa & Rojjanasrirat, 2011). To determine the factor structure of each scale, we relied on the empirical Kaiser criterion, screeplots, and fit indices of exploratory factor analyses. Like in Study 1, a two-factor, five-factor, and two-factor structures were found for the climate hope scale (Ojala, 2015), the ETA-Q (Hahnel & Brosch, 2018), and the awe scale (Bethelmy & Corraliza, 2019), respectively. For the remaining scales, a one-factor structure was adequate. Every factor analysis can be found on the OSF page.

Consent

We asked for participants' consent to participate in this study. If they selected "no", meaning they did not consent to participate, they were sent to the end of the survey.

Eco-Emotions

In this block, we integrated measures from the previous study: Climate hope (ω = [.65, .80]; Ojala, 2015), awe (ω = .70; Bethelmy & Corraliza, 2019), being moved (ω = .84;

Landmann & Rohmann, 2020), the ETA-Q (ω = [.69, .86]; Hahnel & Brosch, 2018), and three single-item measures, pride (from Hahnel & Brosch, 2018), enthusiasm and inspiration (adapted from Hahnel & Brosch, 2018). To extend the replication, we also integrated new eco-emotion measures: Gratitude to nature (ω = .93; Tam, 2022) and Empathy with nature (ω = .92; Tam, 2013). Every response measure ranged from1 = "Completely disagree" to7 = "Completely agree", and the items were in randomized order.

Pro-Environmental Ingroup Identification

In this block, we used the same measure as in Study 1, except that the group, this time, was "environmental activists" (e.g., "I feel close to environmental activists."; Leach et al., 2008). The scale had a very good internal consistency (ω = .92), and items were presented in random order.

Collective Action Intentions

Like in Study 1, we used the measure of Landmann & Rohmann (2020) to assess proenvironmental collective action intentions. Internal consistency was very good (ω = .87), and item presentation was randomized.

Demographics

In the end, we asked participants to report their gender identification, age, political affiliation, education level, income, belief in the environmental crisis, and participation in the previous study. We finally thanked participants, and an email address was displayed if they had encountered any issues or wanted to know the results.

Results

First, given that we have several independent variables (eco-emotions), we ran several mediation models. In addition, as Study 1 was exploratory and the mediation models with ingroup identification were not pre-registered, we corrected our alpha level to a = .001.

In total, we ran 10 mediation models by conducting a joint-significance test (Yzerbyt et al., 2018) and estimating the indirect effect via Monte Carlo simulations with the R package JSmediation (Batailler et al., 2025). The model with constructive hope did not pass the joint-significance test, but the estimated indirect effect was statistically significant at our corrected alpha level. The remaining nine mediation models were statistically significant, meaning that nine out of 10 models were significant. This result is consistent with our statistical power approaching 90%. We summarised the statistics from the mediation models in Table 8. Most models showed medium to large indirect effects, while the constructive hope model exhibited a small one. Regression coefficients are standardized, and their standard errors are in parentheses.

Discussion

In this correlational study, we replicated the mediation effect found in Study 1. That is, the effect of positive and self-transcendent eco-emotions on pro-environmental collective action intentions is mediated by pro-environmental ingroup identification. Even though the hypothesis was the same as in the Social Identity Model of Pro-Environmental Action (Fritsche et al., 2018), we relied on Thomas et al.'s (2009) model that accounts for a more integrative range of affective experiences in predicting collective action intentions. Nine out of 10 mediation models reached significance and exhibited medium to large indirect effects.

Only one mediation model did not reach statistical significance at our corrected alpha level and exhibited a small indirect effect (constructive hope). However, this non-significance is not surprising given our statistical power.

Therefore, these results support the Encapsulation Model of Social Identity of Collective Action (Thomas et al., 2009). Affective experiences highlight identification with a group, and this identification fosters collective action intentions. Our results extend the theory in two ways. First, by extending it to environmental matters. Second, by integrating a larger panel of positive and self-transcendent emotional experiences.

Compared to the original study, we made a few changes. Mainly, we removed some measures (e.g., collective efficacy beliefs, ingroup norms) and kept some (e.g., climate hope), but also added some new eco-emotional measures (e.g., gratitude to nature). In addition, to be very conservative regarding our original effect sizes, we set our alpha level at .001. Despite these changes, we replicated results from Study 1. This is further proof of the robustness of our results.

The present study shared the limitations previously identified in Study 1. To overcome these methodological constraints, as well as the duration issue of the pro-environmental task used in Study 2, we designed a fourth study in which we experimentally induced awe at nature and measured participants' intentions to engage in pro-environmental collective action.

Study 4

Like in Study 2, this study aims to experimentally induce a self-transcendent but different eco-emotion: awe at nature. Awe is defined as an emergent feeling that arises when we encounter something immense in terms of size, quantity, scope, complexity, capacity, or social influence, which transcends our current understanding of the world, the environment, or ourselves (Keltner & Haidt, 2003; Gordon et al., 2017). In this study, we conceptualized awe at nature as a feeling that arises when we encounter a natural scene that is immense in terms of size, quantity, scope, complexity, capacity, or social influence, which transcends our current understanding of the world, the environment, or ourselves. First and foremost, awe was found to be moderately to strongly associated with pro-environmental behavior (Gao, 2026).

Second, in experimental studies, awe moderately influenced pro-environmental behavior intentions (Wang et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2018), and these findings converge with meta-analytical findings (Gao, 2026).

In line with findings of Study 3 and with the Encapsulation Model of Social Identity in Collective Action (Thomas et al., 2009), we hypothesized that inducing awe at nature should produce motivations to engage in pro-environmental collective actions, and this relationship passes through pro-environmental ingroup identification. Specifically, we expect that inducing awe at nature will produce higher intentions to engage in pro-environmental collective actions compared to a control condition. We also expect this relationship to be mediated by identification with environmental activists. That is, inducing awe at nature will produce a higher identification with activists, and this ingroup identification will increase pro-environmental collective action intentions.

Methods

We pre-registered this study in OSF: https://osf.io/65n2b/overview?view_only=b5fd581c1a3642b686629ddd2ad2d573

https://osf.io/65n2b/overview?view_only=b5fd581c1a3642b686629ddd2ad2d573. Any information that was not preregistered will be explicitly mentioned in the article. The data set, analysis scripts, and other related documents can be found on the following link: https://osf.io/x7ebn/overview?view_only=0f7e13d3ddde48f1830086b4b5cc2452.

Power Analysis

We determined a priori what we considered the smallest effect size of interest (i.e., d = 0.3) (Lakens, 2022) for our main effect of interest -the emotional induction effect on collective action intentions. We used a one-factor two-level design comparing a control condition and an experimental condition. Based on this, we carried out a power analysis by doing a two-sided independent t-test, with an alpha of .01 (adjusted for several hypotheses), a power of 80%, and a Cohen's d of 0.3 requires 262 participants per condition. We therefore plan to recruit a total of 530 respondents.

Sample

Participants were from the United Kingdom, recruited via Prolific Academic, and paid £1.6. In total, we collected 600 observations 8 in April 2026. Fifty-eight observations met our exclusion criteria and were removed from the final sample. We therefore ended up with a final sample of 542 participants (Mage = 44.4, SDage = 11.6, 54.9% identified themselves as women, 44.4% identified themselves as men, 0.5% identified themselves as others or preferred not to say).

Procedure & Measures

The experiment was conducted entirely on LimeSurvey. After giving their consent, we assessed participants' commitment to others and participants' connectedness to others (ω = .80 and ω = .77, respectively; Vignoles et al., 2016). Both measures were used for a student's project, were displayed within the same block, and the item order was randomized. Then, participants were randomly assigned to one of the two experimental conditions. Either the control group (n = 278), where participants had to recall a recent memory, or the eco-emotional induction group (n = 264), where participants had to watch a video inducing awe at nature. This eco-emotional manipulation previously showed induction validity (Bellemin et al., 2026). Following the experimental manipulation, we first assessed participants' pro-environmental ingroup identification with a single-item measure (Postmes et al., 2013) and then pro-environmental collective action intentions (ω = .88; Landmann & Rohmann, 2020). Items of collective action were in randomized order. In a previous study, we did not find a significant effect of the awe manipulation on collective action intentions (Bellemin et al., 2026). Before moving on to an actual pro-environmental behavior, we decided to test this hypothesis on intentions again, but with more statistical power. Age and gender questions were displayed at the end of the experiment. We disclosed the real objectives of the study to the participants. They were finally thanked, and an email address was displayed if participants had encountered any issues or wanted to know the results. On average, the experiment lasted approximately 7.5 minutes (SDduration = 3.5).

Results

Given five a priori hypotheses, including the present study and the student's study, we used a Bonferroni correction leading to an alpha level of 1%.

To test our mediation hypothesis, we first tested whether inducing awe at nature influenced intentions to engage in pro-environmental collective actions (total effect). We

Discussion

In this study, we experimentally induced awe at nature and found that it produced higher intentions to engage in pro-environmental collective actions than a control group. In addition, we found that pro-environmental ingroup identification totally accounted for the variance of this emotional induction effect.

This mediation effect is in line with the Encapsulation Model of Social Identity in

Collective Action (Thomas et al., 2009), assuming that affective reactions foster ingroup identification and that identification, in turn, influences engagement in collective actions. This extends the theoretical model to the environmental domain. However, this order of predictors (emotions → ingroup identification → collective action) contradicts the Social Identity Model of Collective Action (van Zomeren et al., 2018 (van Zomeren et al., , 2008)). Thomas et al. (2012, p. 85) argue that this debate of the order of causality is a complex issue that is not necessarily important. They stress the importance of normative alignment between emotions, collective efficacy, and ingroup identification. In the environmental domain, further studies manipulating emotional alignment to a pro-environmental social identity can provide future insights.

The present study also highlights that inducing awe at nature does indeed foster pro-environmental behaviors (intentions in this case), but the effect remains small. This is consistent with meta-analytical findings showing a significant but small effect of awe induction on pro-environmental behaviors (Gao, 2026). Here, we used a nature-based elicitor for awe. We considered this experimental manipulation as manipulating an eco-emotion (Pihkala, 2022; Voşki et al., 2023). One may investigate whether these results would replicate with a manipulation of awe, but one that is not framed as an eco-emotion. For example, whether a human-based elicitor for awe motivates individuals to engage in pro-environmental collective actions.

Limitations concerning this study are very general and will be discussed in the General Discussion.

General Discussion

In this present work, we conducted four pre-registered studies, comprising two correlational designs (Studies 1 and 3) and two experimental designs (Studies 2 and 4). Across Studies 1, 3, and 4, results consistently demonstrated that positive and self-transcendent eco-emotions significantly predicted pro-environmental collective action intentions. We found this previous relationship to be mediated by pro-environmental ingroup identification.

However, this mediation pattern did not replicate when an actual pro-environmental behavior was assessed (Study 2).

These findings lend support to both SIMPEA (Fritsche et al., 2018) and EMSICA (Thomas et al., 2009), suggesting that affective responses related to the environmental crises or the natural environment function as motivational antecedents of pro-environmental behavior (collective actions), and that (pro-environmental) ingroup identification mediates this relationship. Regarding this mediation relationship specifically, EMSICA's rationale may encompass a broad spectrum of emotional responses, including positive and self-transcendent emotions, whereas SIMPEA's rationale appears to place greater emphasis on negative emotional states -though this dimension of the theoretical framework remains largely speculative.

In addition, across the four studies, we consistently found a positive association between pro-environmental ingroup identification and pro-environmental responses, both actual behavior and behavioral intentions. This highlights the importance of considering ingroup identification and, consequently, the added value of social identity theories in the context of the environmental crises. This finding aligns with evidence from both a literature review and a meta-analysis on identity and climate change responses (Mackay et al., 2021; Vesely et al., 2021). Moreover, the fact that the labels for pro-environmental ingroup identification were broad (in Study 1 and 2: "people concerned about the environment") and more specific (in Study 3 and 4: "environmental activists") adds a noticeable value to this robust effect.

In general, we found robust evidence that positive and self-transcendent eco-emotions were related to pro-environmental responses. These present data highlight the relevance of both the positive (Schneider et al., 2021; Schneider, 2025) and self-transcendent eco-emotions pathways in predicting pro-environmental responses (Zelenski & Desrochers, 2021).

Among eco-emotions, environmental trait affect was consistently associated with pro-environmental collective action intentions (Studies 1 and 3) and with donations to a pro-environmental organization (Study 2). Moreover, positive and self-trancendent eco-emotions -operationalized in a trait-like manner in Studies 1 and 3 -were positively correlated with pro-environmental collective action intentions. Considered independently of the remaining findings, this body of evidence supports the proposition that affective attitudes toward environmental crises predict pro-environmental behavior (Landmann, 2020). This relationship may be accounted for by the mechanism of affect generalization (Paolini et al., 2006), whereby the repeated occurrence of eco-emotional episodes gradually consolidates into stable affective attitudes, which in turn constitute more robust predictors of pro-environmental behavior. However, this developmental pathway -through which affect generalization emerges in response to environmental crises -was not directly tested in the present research and therefore remains to be empirically established. Longitudinal designs would appear to be particularly well-suited to examining this process.

Despite the added value of distinct study designs in this research, eco-emotions as trait measures may also raise a question which concerns the difference between state and trait emotions (Fridhandler, 1986). The social identity models of collective actions on which we relied (Fritsche et al., 2018; Thomas et al., 2009; van Zomeren et al., 2018 van Zomeren et al., , 2008) ) do not mention any theoretical assumption on the distinction between emotions as traits and emotions as states. This conceptual difference has clear implications here because eco-emotional measures (in Study 1 and 3) are more trait-like, whereas eco-emotional manipulations (in Study 2 and 4) are more state-like. One limitation of this research is therefore the transposition of findings from correlational studies -in which eco-emotions are operationalized as trait-like affective dispositions -to experimental studies in which eco-emotions are operationalized as state-like affective reactions. We are examining two potentially different constructs here, and the underlying assumptions warrant explicit conceptual justification. We propose that eco-emotions, when measured as traits, capture an affective dimension of pro-environmental social identities -that is, the emotional dispositions characteristic of individuals who identify with environmentally concerned people. As such, the eco-emotional measures employed in the present studies, and in the broader literature, likely reflect stable affective orientations that constitute part of the content of pro-environmental social identities. This raises the possibility that pro-environmental social identity acts as a confounding variable in the observed relationships between eco-emotions and pro-environmental behavior.

Although consistent mediation effects of pro-environmental ingroup identification were observed across Study 1, 3, and 4, all three studies relied on the same measure of behavioral intentions -namely, pro-environmental collective action intentions (Landmann & Rohmann, 2020). This methodological uniformity may constitute a limitation with respect to the external validity of the dependent variable. Future research should seek to replicate these mediation effects using alternative measures of pro-environmental behavioral intentions.

Finally, a sampling issue is at stake in these studies, which can be considered a warning for environmental psychological research. Indeed, despite different recruitment methods, our samples were highly educated and predominantly left-wing 9 . This unbalanced distribution may compromise both generalizability and statistical power by reducing the ability to detect a true effect. (Winkel et al., 2009). We therefore recommend that researchers in environmental psychology exercise particular caution in their sampling strategies to optimize both statistical power and sensitivity.

Conclusion

We hope these studies will help to better understand the role of positive and self-transcendent eco-emotions on pro-environmental responses through group-based processes. In recent years, environmental psychology has seen the emergence of several meta-science and big team projects (e.g., Gago et al., 2024; Vesely et al., 2021; Vlasceanu et al., 2024), and this has to be encouraged to build a solid foundation of knowledge in the field.
